title: Infra: GPU fleet capacity strategy, cloud accounts, IaC modules, CI/CD and runbooks
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

Purpose: This page consolidates Redwood's guidance for GPU fleet capacity planning, cloud account/networking considerations, Terraform/IaC module conventions, CI/CD and build pipeline patterns, and operational runbooks. It is intended for infra engineers, SREs, and platform owners responsible for maintaining predictable GPU inference capacity across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Scope: covers fleet design (pools, SKUs, regions), autoscaling and quota strategies, cloud account and VPC layout, recommended Terraform modules and patterns, CI/CD for infra modules and AMI/container builds, and step-by-step runbooks for capacity incidents and routine capacity operations.

Goals
- Ensure 95th-percentile allocation latency below 120s for normal scale-ups and 99th-percentile below 300s (SLO targets).
- Maintain >99% availability of GPU-backed serving pools during business hours in primary regions.
- Keep cost efficiency by minimizing idle GPU minutes while preserving burst capacity for traffic spikes.

Ownership
- Fleet architecture and IaC modules: infra-fleet team (owner).
- Cloud accounts & networking: cloud-platform team (owner).
- CI/CD pipelines for modules: infra-ci team (owner).
- Oncall for capacity incidents: infra-sre rotation (primary), serving-runtime rotation (secondary).

High-level architecture
- fleet-manager: control plane service that tracks pools, SKUs, and allocations.
- gpu-scheduler: scheduling service that assigns jobs to GPUs with bin-packing heuristics.
- pool-autoscaler: reconciler that adjusts pool size based on target utilization and queued allocations.
- vpc-provisioner: account-scoped module that creates VPCs, subnets, routing, and peering to Redwood control plane for Private deployments.

Capacity planning principles
1) Model-based forecasts: use weekly traffic ingestion + model size map to compute GPU-seconds per model. We keep a 20% safety buffer for unknown bursts.
2) SKU diversity: mix A100-80GB (high throughput), A100-40GB (mid), and H100 (experimental) by workload type. Use quantized variants for cost-sensitive workloads.
3) Regional redundancy: maintain at least 1 warm pool in secondary region with minimal routing weight for failover.
4) Autoscale policies: prefer managed autoscaling with conservative cool-downs; manual override for planned events.

Concrete thresholds and SLOs
- Allocation latency SLO: P95 < 120s, P99 < 300s for requests that require new GPU allocation.
- Pool target utilization: 60-75% (scale-up when > 75% sustained for 5m, scale-down when < 45% for 10m).
- Warm pool minimum: 3 nodes per pool in primary region; 1 node in secondary region for critical tiers.
- Preemptible/spot usage: allow up to 25% of fleet for non-SLA workloads; never use for Dedicated customers.

Cloud accounts & networking
- Account layout: one account per region per environment (prod, staging, dev) with central shared-services account for control plane.
- VPC design: 3 private subnets per AZ, dedicated tech-subnet for GPU instances with stricter NACLs.
- Peering & ingress: control plane connectivity via VPC peering or PrivateLink; use AWS Transit Gateway for multi-region setups.
- IAM guardrails: least privilege roles for pool-autoscaler and provisioning pipelines. Use centralized IAM role-mapping and session-exchange patterns for customer-managed Private deployments.

Terraform / IaC modules (conventions)
- Module naming: modules/compute/gpu-pool, modules/network/vpc, modules/iam/role, modules/launchtemplate/gpu-lt. Keep each module focused and idempotent.
- Versioning: enforce semantic versioning for modules (x.y.z) and release tags in registry. Consumers pin module versions in root stacks.
- Inputs/Outputs: module inputs must be explicit (no implicit provider configs). Outputs limited to values consumers need (id, subnet_ids, instance_profile_arn).
- Example: gpu-pool module usage (Terraform HCL snippet):

terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.2"
}
module "gpu_pool_inference" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-infra/terraform-modules.git//modules/compute/gpu-pool?ref=v1.4.0"
  name   = "inference-prod-eu-west-1"
  sku    = "nvidia-a100-80gb"
  min_nodes = 3
  max_nodes = 100
  instance_profile = module.iam.gpu_instance_profile_arn
  subnets = module.vpc.private_subnets
}

- Tagging: enforce cost center tags, environment, team, and owner tags at module level to support chargeback.
- State management: use remote state in S3 with DynamoDB locking and cross-account access via IAM role assumption.

CI/CD and build pipelines
- Pipeline types:
  - module-publish: validates, lint, unit tests (terraform-compliance), and publishes module to internal registry.
  - infra-deploy: plan and apply against target account using ephemeral pipelines with short-lived credentials.
  - image-build: builds GPU-optimized AMIs and container images; signs artifacts and publishes to ECR/AMI-baking pipeline.
- Gate pattern:
  1) PR + plan (automated)
  2) Automated integration tests against ephemeral environment (smoke: create pool, create allocation, delete)
  3) Manual approval for prod apply (owner + infra-sre)
- Example CLI snippets (jenkins/tekton/gitea pipelines):

# Run terraform fmt & validate
tfenv exec terraform fmt -check && tfenv exec terraform validate

# Run plan with remote workspace
terraform workspace select prod || terraform workspace new prod
terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars -out=plans/prod.plan

Image/canary release guidance
- AMI/image changes that alter instance types or kernel settings require a canary: deploy to 1 AZ (10% of pool) for 2 hours and validate P95 latency and allocation success.
- Rollback policy: automated rollback to previous image if canary exceeds error thresholds (error rate > 1% or P95 allocation latency increased by > 30%).

Runbooks (concise, actionable)
1) Capacity shortage (high-level)
- Symptoms: Allocation API queue grows, allocation latency P95 > 120s, alert: GPU_POOL_HIGH_QUEUED_ALLOCATIONS triggered.
- Immediate actions:
  1. Oncall ack alert.
  2. Check fleet-manager health: curl -sS https://fleet-manager.internal/api/health | jq .status
  3. Inspect pool metrics (Grafana): GPU utilization, queued_allocations, pending_instances.
  4. If autoscaler is inactive: restart pool-autoscaler via k8s rollout restart deployment/pool-autoscaler -n infra
  5. If scale-up is blocked by cloud quotas: open cloud quota request (AWS console -> Support -> Create case) OR use alternative region (runbook step below).
  6. If preemptible churn is causing instability: temporarily reduce spot utilization by setting module tag spot_enabled=false and trigger a rolling resize.
- Escalation: if unable to restore capacity within 30 minutes, page infra-sre lead and product incident commander.

2) Emergency cross-region failover
- Preconditions: secondary warm pool exists and control-plane routing is healthy.
- Steps:
  1. Increase routing weight for secondary region: POST /control-plane/routing/pools/{pool}/weights {"eu-west-2": 20} (use internal API).
  2. Monitor allocation success in secondary region for 10 minutes.
  3. If stable, keep failover for the duration of the event and schedule capacity rebuild in primary region.

3) Routine capacity grow (planned)
- Runbook: planned increase of pool size or new SKU introduction
  1. Create RFC in Change Management template (link: /confluence/policies-and-process/change-management).
  2. Bump Terraform module inputs in infra repo and open PR.
  3. Validate in staging with ephemeral workload (use load-generator job: tools/loadgen/inference-load.yaml).
  4. Schedule maintenance window if required and coordinate with oncall.
  5. Apply to prod with manual approval and monitor.

Monitoring and dashboards
- Dashboards: GPU Fleet Overview, Per-pool latency & queue, SKU utilization, Cloud Quota dashboard.
- Alerts (examples):
  - GPU_POOL_HIGH_QUEUED_ALLOCATIONS: threshold queue_count > 50 for 2m
  - GPU_POOL_LOW_WARM_NODES: warm_nodes < min_nodes for 5m
  - CLOUD_QUOTA_NEARING_LIMIT: used_quota > 85%
- Logs & traces: ensure allocation flows emit trace-id and link to request logs in Kibana.

Testing & validation
- Unit tests for Terraform modules (tflint, terrascan) and integration tests using ephemeral dev accounts.
- Periodic game-days (quarterly) that simulate region outage, quota exhaustion, and IAM key compromise.

Security & compliance considerations
- Use customer-managed KMS for Private deployment AMIs and ensure image inventory is signed.
- Audit logs: record provisioning actions in central CloudTrail and forward to SIEM with 1y retention for infra operations.

Appendix: quick references
- Terraform: remote state pattern example: s3://redwood-terraform-state/<account>-<region>/<stack> with DynamoDB lock table terraform-locks-<env>.
- Common commands:
  # View queued allocations
  curl -sS "https://fleet-manager.internal/api/pools/{pool}/metrics" | jq .queued_allocations

  # Restart autoscaler
  kubectl -n infra rollout restart deployment/pool-autoscaler

  # Resize pool via control-plane API (example)
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"desired_nodes": 50}' https://control-plane.internal/api/pools/inference-prod-eu-west-1/resize

Contacts & escalation matrix
- infra-fleet (owner): infra-fleet@redwood.example.com
- cloud-platform: cloud-platform@redwood.example.com
- infra-sre oncall: infra-sre-oncall@redwood.example.com (pagerduty)

Maintaining this doc
- Owner: infra-fleet team. Review cadence: quarterly or after major incident.
- Update process: open PR against this page (internal markdown source) and add reviewers listed above.
